extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners evaluating patent validity and inventorship)
extracted.subtask_short: assessing patent novelty and public use
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on legal criteria for novelty, public use/sale, abandonment, inventorship, and statutory exceptions relevant to defeating or upholding a patent. Focuses on when prior experiment/use/suggestion bars patentability and who qualifies as the inventor or a protected prior user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use vs completed invention (abandonment test)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention 'rests in experiment and trial' (not completed), acts by the proposer are prima facie experimental and do not constitute a completed invention; long abandonment (e.g., twenty or thirty years) is strong evidence the matter remained experimental rather than a completed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a presumption that uncontinued, abandoned attempts were only experiments. If experiments were continued or there is no satisfactory evidence of abandonment, it becomes a question of fact depending on the nature of the proposed invention, the character of the experiments, and the results attained to determine whether the party had really accomplished the same substantial result as that described in the patent. (See Lord Brougham's test and §45 discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use before patent defeats novelty (use in public)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention publicly used or sold to the public prior to the patent may render the patent invalid — 'if it was used openly in public ... and had continued to use the same thing up to the time of taking out the patent, undoubtedly then ... the plaintiff's invention is not new'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a use is public is a question of fact for the jury; look for manufacture or sale without secrecy such that the public could see it. Public manufacture and sale of articles according to the invention will vitiate subsequent letters patent (cases cited: Jones v. Pearce; Losh v. Hague).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'public use' (use in public, not use by the public)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'public use' means use in public, and not use by the public — e.g., use of a lock in a situation where the public might see it is a public use and exercise of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the machine or article was used or exhibited so that the public could see it. Private or secret use does not ordinarily constitute 'public use' for defeating a patent. (Per Lord Abinger and endorsing notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use must be of a completed invention substantially as patented
rubrics_metrics.description: To count as a public use that defeats a patent, the machine or subject of invention must have been completed and used in public substantially as it was patented, with the consent of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish experimental or incomplete implementations from a completed device used publicly. If the publicly used article is not substantially the same as the patented subject or was merely experimental, it will not necessarily defeat the patent. (§54)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited permission for individual use (experimental allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor permits use by an individual for a short or definite period, as an act of kindness or continuing experiments/testing utility, such limited permission generally will not defeat the patent under the Act of 1836.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the scope and duration of the permission: limited, time-bound licenses or experimental allowances are consistent with preserving patent rights; unlimited or indefinite permission is more likely to constitute abandonment or dedication. (§56)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication/abandonment to the public requires clear, cogent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's acts must be very clear and cogent before a court will conclude he has dedicated his invention to the public and thus forfeited patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts construe inventor's acts liberally in favor of preservation of rights; look for unequivocal conduct such as proclaiming intention to the world and permitting general public use without objection. The question is fact-specific. (§57)

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation or untested theory does not deprive later inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere speculation of a philosopher or mechanician, never tried by experience or put into actual operation, is not an invention that will deprive a subsequent person who reduced it to practice of the reward due to his ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere abstract ideas or untested theories from reductions to practice and actual operable implementations. Practical reduction to use is required to defeat a later patent. (Bedford v. Hunt; Story J.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is the inventor when suggestions or hints are used
rubrics_metrics.description: The law protects the perfected intellectual production — the perfected invention — not the bare suggestion or inchoate idea. Many suggestions or hints may be used by an original genius without invalidating his right; but if the invention was substantially communicated such that the patentee could have applied it in practice 'without more inventive power,' the prior communicator may be the true inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent of contribution: naked idea vs substantial communication of the invention's means. The interval between initial suggestion and final production may reflect inventive effort by the applier; attribution depends on who performed the inventive work to perfect and apply the idea. (§47–48)

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer vs servant inventorship (who is entitled to be inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship depends on the relative situations, the nature of employment, and whether the employer planned or conceived the main idea. If the servant suggested the principle, he is the inventor; if the employer conceived the main idea and the servant only supplied manual dexterity to carry it out, the employer is the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the employer conceived the general principle and merely used the employee's skill to realize it, versus the employee originating the principle. Payment or hiring for inventive work may place the invention in the assignee's hands but facts vary by case. (§49)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which suggestions of workmen affect validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption by an inventor of suggestions made in the course of experiments by workmen (e.g., something more easily carrying conceptions into effect) does not necessarily invalidate the patent if the principal invention stands complete without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the suggestion goes to an essential part of the invention or is merely a trivial or convenient improvement; trivial operational suggestions are unlikely to void the patent. (§51 and related commentary)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of antecedent experiments by later inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments of others not brought to completion will not vitiate a later inventor's patent if the later inventor avails himself of that knowledge and perfects the invention, making it capable of useful operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare U.S. and English approaches: the law will generally allow a successful later inventor to use prior experimental knowledge if he perfects the machine. Determine whether predecessors only experimented without achieving practical completion. (Story J.; §51)

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1839 §7 — prior purchaser/constructor rights and two-year limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act of 1839 provides that any person or corporation who purchased or constructed a newly invented machine, manufacture, or composition of matter prior to the inventor's application shall possess the right to use and vend that specific machine without liability; and no patent shall be invalid by reason of such prior purchase, sale, or use except on proof of abandonment to the public or that such prior purchase/sale/use was more than two years prior to the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a patent issues the prior purchaser retains a right to use the specific machines they purchased/constructed. To claim protection under the statute one must be a purchaser or prior user by license or consent of the inventor — not a purchaser from a mere wrongdoer. If prior use/purchase was for more than two years before application, or there was abandonment, the patent may be invalid. (§58–60)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use must be with inventor's consent/allowance to defeat patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the law, prior public use or sale will defeat a patent only if it was with the knowledge and consent (or allowance) of the inventor before his application; unauthorized use or purely experimental use without consent does not deprive the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine evidence of the inventor's knowledge and assent. Sales or uses in the interval between application and grant do not defeat the patent. Experimental uses to test utility without consent are not treated as public use for disabling the patent. (Wyeth v. Stone; §56)

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchasers from wrongdoers are not protected as prior users
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser who acquired the invention from a wrongdoer (a pirate) cannot claim protection under the Act as a bona fide prior purchaser; a wrongdoer cannot confer valid title under the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though the statute speaks broadly of 'purchasers,' courts will not interpret it to protect those who obtained the invention via fraud, piracy, or gross misconduct. Trace good faith and lawful acquisition when asserting prior-user rights. (Pierson v. The Eagle Screw Company; §60)
